Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Extracting grid characteristics from spatially distributed place cell inputs using non-negative PCA" for peer review at eLife. Your submission has been favorably evaluated by Timothy Behrens (Senior editor), Reviewing editor Michael Frank, and two reviewers.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The authors present analytical and neural network simulations which demonstrate that, under certain constraints, the first principal component of place cell firing patterns in a 2D arena resemble hexagonal grid cell firing patterns. Specifically, these constraints require that the principal components be constrained to non-negativity, and that the place cell inputs have a zero mean in time or space. In addition, they suggest that interesting features of grid cell firing, namely the tendency for grid scale to be discretely clustered, and for the grid to align at approximately 7 degrees to the walls of a square arena. This is an important result which adds to a growing body of recent studies that have emphasised the importance of the projection from place cells to grid cells, as opposed to the grid cell to place cell projection that has been the subject of several previous theoretical studies.

As you will see however, the Reviewers felt that it was important to provide some intuition and cogent explanation about how the results were obtained, and several questions arose along these lines. It is not clear how the dual constraints of (eigenvector) non-negativity and orthogonality are actually satisfied, nor is it clear why they get 7degree alignment or a ratio of 1.4 for the jump in grid scale.

In addition to the revisions articulated below, the following suggestion arose from discussion amongst the Reviewers/editors.

Figure 13 of the manuscript tracks the evolution of the network from different initial conditions.

One might go some way in clarifying the questions of how and why the observed phenomena occur by tracking individual objective measures, in a manner similar to Figure 13.

To wit, one of the algorithms you use trades off two objectives:

(i) maximize the variance of the projection of the data onto the [non-negative] principal component

(ii) enforce approximate orthogonormality by minimizing || I – eT e||, where I is the identity matrix, and e is the normalized "eigenvector," subject to the non-negativity constraint.

In addition, one ought to quantify the degree of non-negativity. There are several ways one might go about this, but one approach would be to normalize the eigenvector to unit length, then take the norm of the vector composed of only the positive entries and subtract the norm of the vector of negative entries.

Essential revisions:

1) This manuscript is of sufficient general interest for publication in eLife, although there is a general lack of detail when describing the methodology. There is also significant overlap with a recent paper at NIPS 2014 (Stachenfeld et al., 2014). I find both papers (Dordek et al., submitted, and Stachenfeld et al.) extremely interesting, and they both have different focusses. But I do think that there needs to be some link to/discussion of Stachenfeld et al.

2) Perhaps the most important issue is that they provide little intuition into the interesting subsidiary results. There is a section on "Why Hexagons?" but none on why other aspects of the results occur. This becomes more important given the fact that Stachenfeld also see the basic result. Why do grid scales have a ratio of 1.4 (indeed is this figure reliable)? Why do they see a non-zero alignment of grids to borders (and is this figure reliable)? Alignment angle appears to depend on place field size, but how does overall place cell firing coverage (and covariance) vary with place field size? How does the alignment angle covary with gridness (the very nice grid-like patterns they show tend to look aligned)?

3) "Due to the isotropic nature of the data (generated by the agent's motion), there was a 2D redundancy in the X-Y plane in conjunction with a dual phase redundancy in 1D, resulting in a fourfold total redundancy of every solution" – this statement requires unpacking. Presumably the dual phase redundancy is caused by the periodic boundary conditions? What are the implications for non-periodic boundary conditions? This sentence needs to be explained to the non-expert reader.

4) Similarly, Figure 4A is cryptic – how does the figure show fourfold redundancy? The authors also use a reduced number of place cells to obtain this result (225 vs. 625 in other simulations) – what are the reasons for this change? This should be explained and justified in the text.

5) More generally, when changing place field size, what happens to the number of place cells – presumably the density of firing overlap (covariance) needs to be maintained as this will strongly affect the results?

6) It is not clear how the non-negative weights are implemented alongside zero mean inputs, and we could not gain any additional insight from the Methods section. This issue needs to be elaborated upon in the text, otherwise it seems implicitly contradictory. Does it imply that the output GC can have negative firing rates? i.e. are there positive and negative place cell firing rates (with a mean of zero), coupled with positive place cell to grid cell synaptic weights, to give both negative and positive inputs to the output grid cell? Presumably the time step to time step changes in grid cell firing rate between negative and positive values will have a large impact on the direction of synaptic weight change – is this the case?

7) Figure 7C, D; also 14B – the analytical PCA results for constrained weights appear to exhibit a bimodal distribution of 90 degree gridness scores – what in the data accounts for this? Can the authors provide any comment or insight?

"The dependency was almost linear" – presumably there is a mathematical reason for this, based on the relationship between the covariance matrix and eigenvectors? Can the authors provide any comment or insight into this relationship?

8) The methods are generally lacking in detail that would allow these simulations to be replicated, based on details provided in the manuscript (see specific details below). The authors should ensure that sufficient detail to allow replication is incorporated. They may also like to consider uploading their code to ModelDB, or a similar online repository, for the sake of transparency and to allow independent replication.

9) The representation of space lies on a torus in this model, which means that the eigenvectors should be periodic and the spatial frequencies quantized. We fail to grasp why, in Figure 3, the first spatial frequency should be 2 and not 1 (i.e., we have two peaks in each direction), and why the eigenvectors 3B is periodic, but in 3A they are not.

10) The eigenvectors of a correlation matrix are orthogonal. If we normalize these eigenvectors and furthermore enforce an additional constraint that the entries of each eigenvector must be positive semidefinite, then the "synaptic weights" of different eigenvectors should not overlap. In other words, if an entry in the first eigenvector is non-zero, it ought to be zero in all other eigenvectors.

11) While the algorithms the authors use relax this last constraint, it is not clear how skewing or shearing a square pattern that results from PCA helps satisfy the dual constraints of non-negativity and orthogonality.

This is a key point in the paper, and begs for an intuitive explanation, or at least more analysis or quantification of the degree to which the constraints are satisfied.

12) The finding that the spacings corresponding to successive eigenvectors obey ~ 2 also calls for an explanation. Why should this ratio of spacings best satisfy non-negativity, orthogonality, and periodicity?

Reviewer #1:

The authors have worked hard to provide further intuition and interpretation to their results, with much success, although there are still some points that should be clarified, see comments below.

There is also a plain error that should be removed. The authors state "the distribution of grid orientations becomes uniform in the range of 0-15 degrees, with a mean (and median) at 7.5 degrees, similar to experimental data [Stensola et al., 2015]". On the contrary the experimental data shows a very non-uniform distribution clearly peaked at about 7.5 degrees, which is quite different. Also, as a circular variable limited to [0,15) – albeit one for which 16 degrees corresponds to 14 degrees rather than 1 degree – the 'mean' and 'median' they refer to are undefined if the distribution is uniform. Thus the authors should acknowledge that they do not provide an explanation for this aspect of the experimental data, and some of the text/ results on this point could be removed, most importantly in the Abstract.

At the start of describing the main result (Results, first paragraph) is not clear that the "1d mapping of the 2d activity" is caused by the trajectory of the rat moving through the place fields.

The next part of the description of their PCA analysis as Eigenvectors and their spatial interpretation could also be improved in terms of intuition. It would be worth mentioning that the PCA, in addition to being calculated as the Eigenvectors of the matrix of temporal covariance between inputs, can also be thought of in terms of singular value decomposition of the (appropriately normalised) input activity. I.e. the input to the network (temporal sequences of place cell activity) can be decomposed into an outer product of (spatial) weights over place cell inputs (their Eigenvectors) and temporally varying weights over these Eigenvectors. The network learns the spatial weights over place cells (the Eigenvectors) as the connections weights from the place cells, and "projection onto place cell space" is simply the firing rates of the output neuron plotted against the location of the rat.

In the second paragraph of the subsection “Adding a non-Negativity constraint to the PCA “it is important to remind the reader that the "raw place cells activity" is not the final input to the PCA numerical methods – spatial or temporal mean normalization has to happen first.

It would be useful to have a surface plot showing Gridness vs. PC Density vs. PC Width. I have found it hard to replicate the Gridness distribution and wonder how general it is to the precise place cell inputs used? The reference to Figure 10A in the third paragraph of the subsection “Effect of place cell parameters on grid structure “is incorrect (I think) – not showing the dependence on the width of the place fields.

Regarding the presence of "modules" of grid cells (subsection “Modules of grid cells”), it is not clear if the interpretation is that different modules correspond to different grid scales, or different Eigenvectors (even if having the same scale). Assuming the latter, it seems that the analysis predicts that there should only be two modules, with the scale of the first module approximately 7.5x the largest place field inputs, and the second module (~2 smaller) existing only to enable non-negative PCA solutions. This deserves discussion, given that the data show at least 5 modules, with a range of scales, the smallest and most numerous having approximately the scale of the smaller place fields found in the dorsal hippocampus (25-30 cm).

results.result: The authors propose a single-layer feedforward neural network with Hebbian learning that connects place cell inputs to grid cell outputs. This architecture resembles neural networks used for Principal Component Analysis (PCA), where the output weights converge to the leading principal component of the input data.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C81-C82 describe the core model architecture and its relationship to PCA. The model is clearly defined with appropriate references to figures (Figure 2), and the connection to PCA is well-established in the literature. The architecture and learning rule are standard and mathematically sound.

results.result: The model produces hexagonal grid patterns when feedforward weights are constrained to be non-negative, but produces square lattice patterns without this constraint. Quantitative gridness scores confirm this: constrained networks achieved gridness of 1.07±0.003 vs 0.302±0.003 for unconstrained networks across ~1500 simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C25-C28, C34 present the central finding with strong quantitative support from extensive simulations (n~1500) and multiple complementary metrics (hexagonal gridness and square gridness scores). The results are consistent across both neural network simulations and direct PCA calculations, with clear statistical differences and appropriate error reporting (SEM). Figures 5-7 provide visual confirmation.

results.result: The model requires zero-mean inputs to produce periodic grid-like outputs. Simple Gaussian place cell inputs fail to generate hexagonal grids, while time-differentiated inputs, Mexican-hat (Laplacian) inputs, or positive-negative disk inputs successfully generate grid patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30, C32-C33, C53 identify a critical requirement for the model. The zero-mean requirement follows from PCA theory (C29), and the empirical tests with different input types (C32-C33, with references to Figures 5, 6, 9) provide clear experimental validation. The negative result with Gaussian inputs and positive results with zero-mean alternatives are well-documented.

results.result: The simulation uses 2D Gaussian functions uniformly distributed to mimic place cell activity. The resulting covariance matrix has Toeplitz structure due to spatial stationarity, becomes circulant with periodic boundary conditions, and shows heavy degeneracy with ~90% variance in the first 15% of eigenvectors and a fourfold grouping pattern in eigenvalues.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 describe the input structure and mathematical properties with appropriate citations (Dai et al., 2009; Gray, 2006) and figure references (Figures 1B, 4A-C). The Toeplitz/circulant structure follows from standard mathematical theory, and the degeneracy is quantitatively documented with clear visual evidence in Figure 4.

results.result: The hexagonal solution is stable across various initial conditions (random, stripes, squares, rhomboids, noisy hexagons) and different trajectories. ODE analysis confirms stability with gridness scores of 1.1±0.0006 (60°) and 0.006±0.002 (90°) for constrained weights.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C38-C39 demonstrate robustness through multiple stability tests. The convergence from diverse initial conditions (C35, Figure 10) and stability across trajectory variations (C36) are well-documented. The ODE analysis (C38-C39) provides theoretical support with quantitative metrics from 60 runs with 400 outputs each.

results.result: Grid spacing shows a linear relationship with place cell field width: S = 7.5σ + 0.85 for periodic boundary conditions. Grid scale depends more on place field size than environment size.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 establish a quantitative relationship between input and output parameters. The linear fit is derived from multiple simulations with clear documentation (Figure 12A), and the relationship is explained analytically in the Methods section. The finding that grid scale depends more on place field size than box size (C43, Figure 12H) is empirically demonstrated.

results.result: Grid orientation varies substantially (0-15°) for different place cell field widths. Analytical considerations predict uniform distribution of orientations in large environments with mean at 7.5°. Grid orientation does not clearly correlate with gridness scores, and gridness exceeds 1 for sufficiently large place cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 characterize grid orientation properties with empirical observations (Figures 12B-D) and analytical predictions (C45). The lack of correlation between orientation and gridness (C46) and the high gridness values for large place cells (C47, Figures 12E-G) are documented, though the analytical prediction of uniform orientation distribution (C45) is noted to conflict with experimental data in C74.

results.result: A hierarchical multi-output network produces two modules of grid cells with different spacings. The ratio between module spacings is approximately 1.4 (close to √2), matching experimental findings (Stensola et al., 2012). The model is limited to producing only two modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 address the module structure with the hierarchical network producing two distinct modules (C50, Figure 14A-B) with spacing ratio ~1.4 (C51) consistent with experimental data. However, the model's limitation to only two modules (C52) is acknowledged as a discrepancy with experimental observations of 5+ modules (see C72), which limits the biological relevance of this finding.

results.result: The grid spacing ratio between consecutive modules is approximately 1.4 (√2), consistent with experimental measurements by Stensola et al. (2012).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C51, C70-C71 report agreement between model predictions and experimental data. The ratio of ~1.4 is consistently reported across different analyses (abstract and hierarchical network results) and explicitly compared to experimental findings (Stensola et al., 2012). This represents a successful quantitative prediction of the model.

results.result: The model shows discrepancies with experimental data: it predicts only two modules while experiments show at least 5 modules, and it predicts uniform grid orientation distribution (0-15°) while experiments show a peak at 7.5°.
results.evaluation: Claims C72 and C74 honestly acknowledge limitations of the model. The discrepancy in module number is clearly stated with reference to experimental data (C72), and the orientation distribution mismatch is explicitly noted with citation (Stensola et al., 2015). These are important limitations that affect the model's biological realism.

results.result: The non-negative PCA optimization problem is NP-hard, requiring numerical methods. The neural network implementation provides a practical advantage for solving this problem.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 correctly characterize the computational complexity (with citation to Montanari and Richard, 2014) and note the practical utility of the neural network approach. This is a valid observation about the computational aspects of the model, though C57 notes this should be investigated further.

results.result: Analytical analysis shows that hexagonal patterns maximize grid cell output variance under non-negativity constraints. In Fourier space, the solution is a hexagonal lattice with lattice constant near the peak of the Fourier transform of the place cell tuning curve.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 present key theoretical insights from the analytical work detailed in the Materials and methods section. The Fourier space analysis (C78, Figures 15-16) provides mathematical explanation for why hexagonal patterns emerge. The analysis is mathematically rigorous and provides mechanistic understanding of the numerical results.

results.result: The model makes several testable predictions: (1) grid cells must receive zero-mean input, potentially through lateral inhibition; (2) place-to-grid weights should be similar across identically-spaced grid cell populations; (3) linear relationship between place cell size and grid spacing; (4) grid spacing determined by largest place cells; (5) uniform grid orientation distribution in large environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69, C73 present predictions derived from the model. These are logical consequences of the model structure and analytical results. However, some predictions (particularly C73 regarding orientation) are already known to conflict with experimental data (C74), which should temper confidence in untested predictions.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior work on grid cell models, noting that most assume velocity input and path integration, while recent experimental evidence supports the importance of feedback from place cells to grid cells, including developmental and inactivation studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C13-C18 provide context from prior literature with appropriate citations. The characterization of existing models (C13-C15) and the experimental evidence for place-to-grid feedback (C16-C18) are well-supported by citations (Bonnevie et al., 2013; Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010). This establishes the motivation for the current work.

results.result: The manuscript cites established anatomical and physiological knowledge about the spatial navigation system, including the locations of place cells, grid cells, and other cell types, as well as the excitatory nature of hippocampus-to-MEC projections and the prevalence of Mexican-hat transformations in the nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12, C24, C31, C54 present well-established neuroscience knowledge with appropriate citations. These are background facts that provide biological context for the model. The citations are appropriate and the statements are consistent with current understanding of the spatial navigation system.

results.result: The manuscript positions the current work relative to prior modeling efforts, noting that Stachenfeld et al. (2014) also connected grid cells to place cells via PCA but produced square grids due to lack of non-negativity constraint. The authors claim novelty in identifying the importance of non-negativity and zero-mean requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 appropriately cite and critique related work (Stachenfeld et al., 2014; Franzius et al., 2007; Kropff and Treves, 2008; Castro and Aguiar, 2014; Stepanyuk, 2015). The claim of novelty (C63-C64) regarding the non-negativity constraint and zero-mean requirement appears justified based on the cited literature, though the strength of this claim depends on thorough literature review.

results.result: Prior theoretical work has shown that hexagonal grids are optimal for spatial coding: Mathis et al. (2015) demonstrated they maximize spatial resolution using Fisher information, and Wei et al. (2013) showed they minimize the number of neurons needed for a given resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 accurately cite prior theoretical work on the optimality of hexagonal grids. These citations provide important context for why hexagonal patterns might be biologically preferred, complementing the current work's mechanistic explanation for how they arise.

results.result: The work demonstrates that grid cells can form from a Hebbian neural network with place cell inputs without path-integration mechanisms, and that the required inhibitory connectivity between grid cells is consistent with known anatomy.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 present the main conclusion of the paper. This is supported by the extensive simulation results (C6-C7, C25-C28, C34-C36) and analytical work (C77-C78). The consistency with anatomical data (C80, citing Couey et al., 2013) strengthens the biological plausibility. However, the discrepancies noted in C72 and C74 indicate the model is incomplete.

results.result: Mexican-hat place cell inputs could result from interactions between place cells and inhibitory interneurons in the hippocampal network.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is explicitly speculative ("could be a result") with citation support (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996). While the speculation is reasonable given the known abundance of inhibitory interneurons, no direct evidence is provided for this specific mechanism. This remains a hypothesis requiring experimental validation.
